chapter_theme: Songs at Uttaramerur (உத்தரமேரூர், வடமேரு): the poet asks to know by inner knowledge the feet that all the gods and sages fail to know, to be rid of the body built of skin and phlegm, to be looked on despite a life spent chasing women and wealth and singing for worthless men, and to be freed from the sea of desire; one praise recalls Siva claiming Sundarar as his slave.

714.reading: The poet lists those who seek and cannot know the Lord's feet, the Vedas, the guardians of the eight directions, the seven rishis, the three lights, the nine Naths, the star-worlds, the priests, a crore of sects and hundreds of crores of gods, and asks that he, a servant, be given the knowledge that knows within knowledge, so that he may know them. The praise is a battle: mountains turn to powder, the sea to mud, Sura dies, ghouls dance, dogs, jackals and crows feed on rivers of blood, and even Yama bows, as Murugan rides the peacock, lord of the gods at Vada Meru.
714.nuance: அறிய அறிய அறியாத அடிகள் ... அறிவுள் அறியும் அறிவு: the feet that all knowing fails to know are to be known by a knowing within knowing, given by grace. The long list of seekers is there to set off the poet's 'even I' (அடியேனும்).

715.reading: The poet speaks of the gross body built of skin, bone, pus, nerves, rheum and phlegm, rolled into a lump, which he carries uselessly and wastes in, and asks whether, his sickness and sorrow gone, he will think of the feet praised by Siva, Vishnu, Brahma, the Vedas and Agamas, and of the six faces, twelve shoulders and victorious vel. The praise names Murugan son of the goddess who wears the crescent and is the form of Vedic mantra, the one who dwells in the five mayas, five elements and five nadas and all that moves and stays, who embraced the hunter girl when the elephant frightened her, at Meru Mangai.
715.nuance: தூல பங்க காயம்: the 'gross' body, a technical word that implies the subtle body beside it. The elephant that frightens Valli into Murugan's arms is Ganesha helping his brother.

716.reading: The poet confesses that he fell in love with long-haired women and lost his way, ran over the earth seeking wealth until his heart withered, never thought justly of the life in Siva, and, a deceiving sinner, made a crore of songs giving names to what only feeds ruin; he asks how he will live, and whether Murugan will not look on him with the gaze he has for his devotees. The praise names Uttaramerur, where Vishnu, Brahma, those who know the Agamas, Ganesha, jnanis and the twelve hundred Vedic priests dwell, and Murugan who came there on the peacock, whose vel burned Sura to ash, the lord of the deer's daughter.
716.nuance: பாழினுக்கு இரையாய நாமம் வைத்து ஒருகோடி பாடல்: I read this as the poet's regret at having sung praise of perishable men or things, a confession about his own art; the line could be divided otherwise. ஆயிரத்திருநூறு மறையோர் is a local detail of the shrine.

717.reading: The poet tells how, infatuated by women's breasts and pearl strings, fragrant hair, carp-like eyes, feet, waist and crescent foreheads, he is ruined and wanders daily in the sea of desire, and asks the twelve-shouldered master of a thousand arts to grant grace to him who wanders as a man of the middle sort. The praise names Murugan the treasure of Siva, who came with a deed into the assembly, called a madman and asked for his answer, and by that just stratagem claimed faultless Sundarar for his own, and the lord of Meru Mangai, home of priests of true Tamil, with its Vedas and sacrifices.
717.nuance: சாதனங்கொடு ... பித்தா ... சுந்தரனைத் தான் ஒற்றிகொள்: the story of Siva appearing with a bond to claim Sundarar as his hereditary slave, in which Sundarar called him பித்தா. It is the book's model of service by claim (thondu). மத்திபன் may mean a middling or mediocre man, and the lines on the priests who establish Vedas and sacrifices are hard to divide.
